summary: THE LAST SIGNAL is an interactive e-flip space magazine for young explorers that tells the stories of NASA spacecraft left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Readers flip through a digital magazine and pick a world. In each five-page chapter the spacecraft itself talks to the reader in the first person and answers five questions: Who am I? What kind of spacecraft am I? Where and how was I launched? What did I discover? Why was I left behind? The Moon section features Eagle (Apollo 11), Intrepid and ALSEP (Apollo 12), Falcon (Apollo 15) and Surveyor 3; the Mars & beyond section features Sojourner, Spirit & Opportunity, Ingenuity and Kepler. Every chapter has a launch video and a mini game: a Moon buggy driving game, a matching game, quizzes, an ID-card builder and a chat with Ingenuity. By turning "discarded equipment" into characters with feelings and stories, the project shows children that these machines are not forgotten junk but silent witnesses of human curiosity, and makes NASA mission history fun to explore.
details:
WHAT IT DOES THE LAST SIGNAL is a web-based e-flip magazine ("Space Magazine for Young Explorers") about eight NASA spacecraft that completed their missions and were left behind: Eagle (Apollo 11), Intrepid/ALSEP (Apollo 12), Falcon (Apollo 15) and Surveyor 3 on the Moon; Sojourner, Spirit & Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars; and the Kepler space telescope, still orbiting the Sun.

HOW IT WORKS The reader opens the cover, picks the Moon or Mars, and turns pages like a real magazine (drag a page corner or use the navigation buttons). A clickable table of contents jumps to any spacecraft. Each spacecraft has a five-page chapter written in the first person ("Hello, little space explorer! My name is Eagle..."): 1. Who am I? 2. What kind of spacecraft am I? (its parts explained simply) 3. Where and how was I launched? (with a launch video) 4. What did I discover? 5. Why was I left behind? Each chapter ends with a mini game that reinforces what the child read: Moon Buggy Rally (drive the Apollo 15 rover 27.9 km, jump craters, collect rock samples, then answer the hammer-and-feather question), an ALSEP matching game, "Space Detective: Who Am I?" and Sojourner quizzes, a Spirit & Opportunity clue game with an ID-card builder and badge, a "Meet Ingenuity" chat, and a Kepler junior academy quiz.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT - Answers the challenge by turning equipment that is usually seen as "space junk" into storytelling characters, so children understand why it was left behind and what it achieved. - Teaches real mission facts (dates, landing sites, sample masses, distances, discoveries) using NASA sources, in language children can follow. - Learning by playing: every story is followed by an interactive game, which keeps attention and helps memory. - Works in any modern browser on phones, tablets and computers, with no installation, so schools and families can use it for free. - Can be expanded with new "issues" (more lost signals) and translated into other languages.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES HTML5, CSS3 (container-query responsive layout) and JavaScript; StPageFlip (page-flip) library for the page-turning effect; HTML5 Canvas for the Moon Buggy game; hand-coded SVG illustrations (cover, planets, rovers, badge); embedded MP4 launch videos. NASA mission pages and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal were used for facts. Generative AI (Claude) was used to help write code and text, as disclosed in the project.

CREATIVITY - First-person narration: each machine "speaks" to the child, which creates empathy and turns history into a personal story. - A real magazine experience in the browser (cover, contents, section dividers, page flipping) instead of a regular website. - Connected stories: Apollo 12 landed 180 m from Surveyor 3 and brought its parts home, so the reader meets the same robot from two sides. - Each game is tied to a real event (driving 27.9 km on the Moon, Opportunity's 45 km record, Ingenuity's 72 flights).

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED Age-appropriate language and a colorful design for children; scientific accuracy checked against NASA sources; mobile and touch support; short pages so children are not overwhelmed; a consistent five-question structure so children know what to expect; and no use of NASA logos or branding.
